objective_for_doctor: Assess and diagnose the patient presenting with a scalp and forehead rash.

turns.content: Doctor: I’m Dr. Agent—let’s get to the cause of your scalp/forehead rash. First: when did it start, and is it itchy, painful, or burning? Doctor: Any recent triggers—new hair products/medications, sun exposure, sick contacts, or recent travel?

Doctor: I’m Dr. Agent—when did the rash start, and is it itchy, painful, or burning? Patient: It started when he was a few weeks old, and it mainly looks red and scaly with greasy yellow scales on his scalp and forehead; he seems comfortable and the parents haven’t noticed significant itching or pain. Doctor: Any recent triggers—new hair products, medications, sun exposure, sick contacts, or recent travel? Patient: There haven’t been new products or medicines, and we haven’t traveled; the rash seems to flare more during cold weather.

Dr. Agent: Thanks—this sounds like a chronic infant facial/scalp process with greasy yellow scale and worsening in cold weather; can you tell me if there are any thick diaper-area rashes, skinfold redness, or if it involves the eyebrows/behind the ears? Dr. Agent: Also, is there any oozing, cracks around the mouth, fever, or swollen/tender areas on the scalp (or any hair loss)?

Doctor: Any thick diaper-area rash, redness in skinfolds, involvement of the eyebrows or behind the ears, oozing or cracks around the mouth, fever, or swollen/tender areas on the scalp with hair loss? Patient: The parents haven’t noticed significant diaper-area or skinfold redness, and it seems mainly on the scalp and forehead; no oozing, mouth cracks, fever, or tender/swollen scalp areas, and they haven’t seen any hair loss.

Doctor: Given greasy yellow “crust” on the scalp/forehead starting in infancy and flaring in cold weather, I’m leaning toward seborrheic dermatitis; can you confirm if it involves the eyebrows/behind the ears at all and whether there are patches elsewhere (like chest/back)? Doctor: If you can, also tell me if the rash improves with gentle washing/keratolytic baby shampoo (even temporarily) or if it’s completely refractory. DIAGNOSIS READY: Seborrheic dermatitis of infancy (cradle cap).
